item.title: Podcast: Why We Trust Online Reviews
item.summary: A podcast host explains social proof, why online reviews can be manipulated, and four habits for reading them critically.
item.transcript_text: Welcome back to the show. Before you booked your last hotel, or chose a restaurant, or bought a phone case, I'd guess that you read the reviews. Most of us do, and it's worth asking why we trust the opinions of complete strangers so readily. Psychologists use the term social proof for this. When we're unsure what to do, we look at what other people have done and assume they knew something we don't. In a busy market, that's often a sensible shortcut. A crowded café is probably crowded for a reason. The trouble is that social proof can be manufactured. Some businesses pay for glowing reviews, or offer discounts in exchange for five stars, and some reviews are simply written by the owner's cousin. So how do you read reviews without being fooled? Well, a few habits help. First, ignore the average score and read the middle reviews, the threes and the fours. They tend to be more detailed and less emotional than the extremes. Second, look for specifics. 'Amazing place, best ever' tells you almost nothing, whereas 'the room was quiet but the wifi kept dropping' sounds like someone who was actually there. And if a reviewer mentions a problem, see whether the business replied, and how; a calm, helpful reply often tells you more than the complaint itself. Third, check the dates. A sudden wave of perfect reviews in a single week should make you suspicious. And finally, remember that every review describes someone else's experience, shaped by their own expectations. A hotel that one guest calls far too quiet might be exactly what you're looking for.
